Whether the spin-on oil filter has a faulty anti-drainback valve
rationale: Many engines mount the spin-on oil filter horizontally or inverted and rely on an internal rubber/silicone anti-drainback valve inside the filter to keep oil from draining out of the upper oil galleries back into the pan after shutoff. A defective anti-drainback valve forces the oil pump to refill the empty filter and galleries on every startup, causing a 2–3 second dry-start bearing/timing-tensioner rattle and delayed oil pressure light extinguish.

question: All of the following diagnostic methods can be used to locate an external intake manifold vacuum leak on a running gasoline engine EXCEPT:
options: Performing a wet cranking compression test by squirting 10W-30 oil into each cylinder spark plug hole
Monitoring Short-Term Fuel Trim (STFT) PIDs on a scan tool while selectively directing small amounts of propane around suspected intake gasket seams
Listening around intake runner joints and vacuum fittings with an ultrasonic leak detector or a length of rubber hose held to the ear
Introducing automotive diagnostic smoke into the sealed intake manifold with the engine off and looking for escaping smoke around gaskets and hoses
rationale: A wet cranking compression test (A) evaluates mechanical sealing inside the combustion chamber (piston rings vs. valves/head gasket) with the throttle held wide open; it cannot detect external intake manifold vacuum leaks. Smoke testing (D), STFT enrichment reaction with propane (B), and acoustic/ultrasonic listening (C) are all effective ways to pinpoint intake vacuum leaks.

question: A technician is diagnosing a 4-cylinder engine that lacks power and has a rhythmic popping sound in the exhaust. The technician performs a running compression test and records the following data: Cylinder #1 (Cranking 170 psi | Running Idle 65 psi | WOT Snap 136 psi), Cylinder #2 (Cranking 168 psi | Running Idle 64 psi | WOT Snap 134 psi), Cylinder #3 (Cranking 172 psi | Running Idle 66 psi | WOT Snap 138 psi), and Cylinder #4 (Cranking 195 psi | Running Idle 115 psi | WOT Snap 175 psi). Why are the cranking, idle running, and WOT snap pressures on Cylinder #4 all significantly higher than on Cylinders #1, #2, and #3?
options: A severely worn exhaust cam lobe on Cylinder #4 failing to evacuate exhaust gas
A bent intake valve on Cylinder #4 stuck partly open on the compression stroke
Broken top and second compression rings on the Cylinder #4 piston
Stripped spark plug threads in the Cylinder #4 aluminum cylinder head port
rationale: During a running compression test, when an exhaust camshaft lobe wears severely flat (low lift), the cylinder can still draw in a full air charge on the intake stroke, but the barely opening exhaust valve cannot evacuate the trapped charge during the exhaust stroke. The residual trapped pressure compounds with the incoming charge on consecutive cycles, causing anomalously high running compression readings (115 psi idle / 175 psi WOT) alongside intake reversion popping.

question: A customer complains of a low-frequency droning vibration at 2,400 RPM that is felt throughout the cabin even when revving the engine in Park or Neutral. All cylinders have 180 psi compression and zero misfires. While inspecting underneath the vehicle, the technician notices the rubber insulator pads on two engine mounts have collapsed completely so the steel engine bracket is resting metal-to-metal against the front subframe, and an aftermarket rigid exhaust downpipe is touching the transmission crossmember. Technician A says metal-to-metal contact from collapsed engine mounts or grounded exhaust pipes transmits normal engine firing impulses directly into the unibody structure as a harsh vibration/drone. Technician B says loosening and neutralizing (re-centering) stressed engine and transmission mounts at idle before retightening them can often reduce idle vibration. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Both technicians are correct. Even a mechanically perfect engine generates normal firing and reciprocating vibrations that must be isolated from the chassis by compliant rubber/hydraulic mounts and flexible exhaust hangers. Collapsed mounts, grounded exhaust pipes, or mounts tightened under binding tension bypass that isolation and transfer harsh vibration directly into the cabin.

question: A technician is performing a relative compression test using a digital storage oscilloscope (DSO) and a high-amp inductive current clamp placed around the battery cable while cranking the engine with fuel disabled. Five of the six current peaks on the waveform reach 185 amps, while one peak drops to only 105 amps on every revolution of the camshaft. What does that low current peak indicate?
options: One port fuel injector winding has excessive electrical resistance
One copper commutator bar inside the starter motor armature has an open circuit
One cylinder has low mechanical compression requiring less cranking torque
One cell inside the 12-volt lead-acid storage battery is internally shorted
rationale: Starter motor amperage draw is directly proportional to the mechanical load opposing crankshaft rotation. Every time a healthy cylinder compresses air, starter current spikes (~185 A). When a cylinder has low or zero compression, the starter spins through that stroke easily with minimal current draw (~105 A), appearing as a missing or low peak once every 720 degrees of crank rotation.

question: When performing a relative compression test with a dual-trace digital storage oscilloscope (DSO) and an inductive amp clamp on the battery cable, one of the six current peaks is 80 amps lower than the other five. How can the technician identify which specific cylinder corresponds to the low current peak without removing all six spark plugs?
options: Unplug the electronic throttle body actuator connector while cranking
Disconnect the alternator B+ output charging cable and repeat the cranking test
Multiply the battery open-circuit voltage by the peak starter amperage draw
Trigger channel two off the #1 coil pulse and count through the firing order
rationale: By connecting Channel 2 of the lab scope to a known cylinder reference trigger (such as the #1 ignition coil primary/command trigger or inductive clamp on #1 plug wire) while recording starter current on Channel 1, the technician can identify Cylinder #1's compression peak and simply count along the engine's firing order (e.g., 1-2-3-4-5-6) to pinpoint the exact weak cylinder in seconds.

question: A technician is diagnosing a loud clattering sound coming from the front timing chain cover of a V6 engine that is worst at hot idle (when oil pressure is at its lowest) and quietens slightly when engine speed is raised to 2,000 RPM (raising oil pressure). Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?
options: A stretched timing chain with a leaking tensioner or worn guides
Excessive wrist pin-to-piston pin boss clearance in Cylinder #1
A cracked harmonic balancer inner hub keyway on the crankshaft snout
A loose torque converter-to-flexplate bolt inside the bellhousing
rationale: Many overhead-cam engines use pressurized engine oil to actuate the hydraulic timing chain tensioner plunger. If the chain is stretched, the plastic guide rails are worn through, or the tensioner's internal ratcheting lock fails and leaks oil pressure at hot idle, the slack timing chain whips and rattles loudly against the front cover until higher RPM increases oil pressure.

question: An engine suddenly develops heavy blue exhaust smoke at all speeds and a misfire on Cylinder #2. A cranking compression test on Cylinder #2 reads 85 psi dry and only rises to 92 psi wet. Using a borescope inserted through the Cylinder #2 spark plug hole with the piston at BDC, the technician sees two deep, parallel vertical gouges machined straight up and down the thrust side of the cylinder wall, while the valves and piston crown are intact. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A blown cylinder head gasket between Cylinder #2 and the external block edge
Worn intake valve stem oil seals allowing oil to drip onto the back of the intake valve
A dislodged wrist pin circlip allowing the pin to slide out and score the bore
Overheating caused by a cooling system thermostat stuck in the closed position
rationale: On a full-floating wrist pin assembly, if a retaining circlip (or press-fit pin) comes loose, the hardened steel wrist pin shifts axially until its ends rub directly against the cylinder wall. This machines two deep parallel vertical trenches up and down the bore at pin height—so deep that squirting oil during a wet compression test cannot seal the gouges (85 psi dry / 92 psi wet) while pumping massive amounts of oil past the rings.

question: A technician is called to inspect an engine that has creamy, milky-brown froth ("mayonnaise") coating the underside of the oil filler cap only, while the engine oil on the dipstick is completely clean, clear amber, and at the normal full mark. The coolant reservoir level has not dropped over the past 6 months, and the vehicle is driven exclusively on 2-mile neighborhood trips in cold winter weather. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: The cast-iron cylinder block has a major internal crack between the main oil gallery and cooling jacket
Normal moisture condensation fails to boil off during short cold trips and collects in the cap
The multi-layer steel cylinder head gasket is completely blown across all cylinders simultaneously
Automatic transmission fluid is leaking through the radiator cooler directly into the engine crankcase
rationale: Water vapor is a normal byproduct of hydrocarbon combustion that enters the crankcase in small amounts via blow-by. When a vehicle is driven only a few miles in cold weather, the oil never gets hot enough (~212°F / 100°C) for long enough to boil off the moisture so the PCV system can purge it. The rising water vapor condenses inside the coolest plastic/metal point at the top of the engine (the oil filler neck/cap) as milky froth, even while the sump oil on the dipstick remains clean and zero coolant is lost.

question: When performing a wet and dry cranking compression test on a horizontally opposed (boxer) 4-cylinder engine or a V8 engine with slanted cylinders, why should the technician avoid squirting more than one teaspoon (~5 mL) of oil into the cylinder for the wet test?
options: More than one teaspoon of motor oil chemically dissolves the cast-iron cylinder wall crosshatch
Excess oil reduces chamber clearance volume, inflating psi readings and risking hydrolock
Liquid motor oil conducts high-amperage current that shorts out the starter motor windings
Excess motor oil causes the neoprene compression gauge adapter hose to swell shut
rationale: Because liquid oil is incompressible, adding too much oil (e.g., several tablespoons) physically takes up space inside the combustion chamber clearance volume—artificially raising the static compression ratio and masking a leaking valve on horizontally opposed or slanted cylinders where oil can also pool directly around the valve head. One teaspoon (~5 mL, or 2–3 squirts from an oil can) is sufficient to coat the ring pack without distorting chamber volume.

question: A V8 engine equipped with cylinder deactivation (Active Fuel Management / Multi-Displacement System) develops a dead misfire on Cylinder #4 and a loud valvetrain tick immediately after exiting the highway. Static cranking compression on Cylinder #4 is 170 psi, but running compression at idle on Cylinder #4 is 0 psi, and removing the valve cover reveals that the Cylinder #4 intake rocker arm does not move at all while the engine is idling. The camshaft lobe is inspected via borescope and is in perfect condition. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The Cylinder #4 piston compression rings are stuck in their ring grooves
The primary timing chain at the front of the engine has broken in half
The Cylinder #4 intake valve head has broken off and fallen into the cylinder
The cylinder deactivation lifter on Cylinder #4 is mechanically stuck collapsed
rationale: Cylinder deactivation (AFM/MDS) lifters use oil-pressure-actuated spring-loaded locking pins generated by the VLOM solenoid manifold to unlatch the outer lifter body from the inner plunger, allowing the outer body to telescope up and down without opening the valve. If the locking pins bind or a return spring breaks, the lifter remains stuck in its collapsed state even when all-cylinder mode is commanded, resulting in zero valve lift despite an intact camshaft lobe.

question: All of the following are valid safety or procedural precautions when performing a cylinder leakage (leak-down) test EXCEPT:
options: Ensuring the vehicle is in Park (or Neutral with the parking brake set) and keeping hands and wrenches clear of the crankshaft pulley before applying compressed air
Running the engine at 2,500 RPM while compressed shop air is connected to the spark plug hole
Positioning the piston of the cylinder being tested at exact TDC on its compression stroke
Removing the radiator cap, oil filler cap, and air intake duct so escaping air can be heard or seen clearly
rationale: A cylinder leakage (leak-down) test is strictly a static test performed with the engine OFF and the piston held stationary at TDC on the compression stroke. Attempting to run the engine with a leak-down tester threaded into a spark plug hole (B) is impossible and dangerous.

question: While inspecting a failed turbocharged engine with a melted hole burned through the center of the #2 piston crown, the technician finds a non-OEM spark plug installed in Cylinder #2 whose heat range is three steps hotter than factory specification, with its ground electrode melted away. Which abnormal combustion phenomenon occurred in Cylinder #2, and how does it differ from normal spark knock (detonation)?
options: Normal spark knock; two flame fronts collided harmlessly after Top Dead Center without raising piston crown temperature
Post-ignition; the fuel mixture failed to ignite until the exhaust valve opened, cooling the piston crown excessively
Diesel runaway; engine oil from the crankcase ignited inside the muffler after leaving the cylinder
Pre-ignition; the glowing plug tip ignited the mixture BEFORE the timed ignition spark
rationale: Pre-ignition occurs when an incandescent hot spot inside the combustion chamber (such as an overly hot spark plug insulator, sharp valve margin, or glowing carbon deposit) ignites the air-fuel charge BEFORE the spark plug fires, while the piston is still moving upward on the compression stroke. Compressing an already burning charge drives cylinder temperatures and pressures sky-high, rapidly melting a hole through the aluminum piston crown. (By contrast, detonation/spark knock occurs AFTER the spark plug fires, when unburned end-gas auto-ignites).

question: A technician is checking an aluminum 4-cylinder cylinder head for warpage using a precision straightedge and feeler gauges. In which patterns must the straightedge be placed across the cylinder head deck surface?
options: Only along the outer intake and exhaust manifold mounting flange rails
Diagonally corner-to-corner, longitudinally along the deck, and transversely
Only across the recessed combustion chamber domes using a depth micrometer
Around the outer perimeter head bolt bosses using an outside micrometer
rationale: Standard cylinder head warpage inspection requires laying a precision straightedge across the deck in at least five positions: both diagonals (X-pattern), longitudinally down the center and edges, and transversely across the width between cylinders, checking beneath the straightedge with a feeler gauge.

question: When resurfacing an aluminum cylinder head that will be installed with a Multi-Layer Steel (MLS) head gasket, Technician A says the surface roughness average (RA) must be much smoother (typically 15–30 microinches RA) than what is required for a traditional composite gasket. Technician B says using a coarse rotary abrasive conditioning disc in a die grinder is the recommended way to prepare the deck for an MLS gasket. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Technician A is correct: MLS gaskets are made of embossed spring-steel layers that require a very smooth, flat mirror-like finish (typically 15–30 RA) to seal properly. Technician B is incorrect: rotary abrasive bristle/pad discs gouge aluminum, create low spots, and leave abrasive grit in oil passages, ruining the flatness required for MLS gaskets.

question: What is the correct sequence and procedure for removing cylinder head bolts from an aluminum overhead-cam (OHC) cylinder head to prevent warping the casting?
options: Cool to room temperature, then loosen bolts from the outer ends inward
Loosen bolts immediately on a hot engine, starting at the center and spiraling outward
Loosen all intake-side head bolts completely first, followed by all exhaust-side bolts
Remove bolts in one pass with a high-torque impact wrench moving in a clockwise circle
rationale: Aluminum heads will warp severely if unbolted while hot. Furthermore, while tightening a cylinder head always starts in the center and spirals outward, loosening/removal is performed in the reverse order (starting at the outer ends and working inward toward the center in 2–3 progressive steps) so the center bolts don't bow the ends of the casting upward.

question: A technician is inspecting a set of removed valve springs. All of the following tests are performed to verify valve spring serviceability EXCEPT:
options: Measuring spring squareness using a carpenter's/machinist's try square on a surface plate
Measuring spring free height with a vernier caliper
Measuring spring coil wire resistance with a digital multimeter
Measuring spring tension (open and closed load in pounds) at specified heights using a spring tester
rationale: Valve springs are inspected for free length, out-of-squareness (rotating the spring against a right-angle square on a flat surface plate), and spring pressure (lbs at specified compressed height). Electrical resistance has no relation to mechanical valve spring condition.

question: After grinding or machining a valve seat and resurfacing the valve face during a cylinder head rebuild, the valve sits deeper (recessed further) into the combustion chamber head casting. How does this affect valve spring installed height and valve stem tip height?
options: Valve spring installed height increases, reducing closed valve spring tension
Valve spring installed height decreases, causing coil bind
Valve spring installed height remains unchanged
On a pushrod engine with hydraulic lifters, lifter plunger preload decreases (more clearance)
rationale: When material is removed from the valve seat and face, the valve moves deeper into the guide toward the rocker arm/camshaft. This pushes the valve stem tip and retainer higher up away from the spring pocket, increasing the valve spring installed height and reducing spring tension. Calibrated valve spring shims are placed under the spring to restore proper installed height.

question: During a valve job, a technician lightly coats the valve face with Prussian Blue, inserts the valve into the guide, and rotates it 1/4 turn against the valve seat with light pressure. Where should the blue contact ring appear on the valve face?
options: Centered on the middle of the valve face with an even width all around
Directly on the very top edge (margin) of the valve head
At the bottom edge of the valve face closest to the valve stem
On only half of the circumference of the valve face
rationale: Proper valve-to-seat contact should form an unbroken, uniform ring centered near the middle of the valve face (and within the specified seat width, typically 0.040"–0.060" for intake and 0.060"–0.080" for exhaust) to maximize heat transfer and prevent burning the margin.

question: When inspecting a resurfaced intake valve, a technician measures the valve margin (the flat cylindrical rim between the valve head surface and the angled face) and finds it is 0.012 in. (0.30 mm) thick. The minimum specification is 1/32 in. (0.031 in. / 0.80 mm). What will happen if this valve is reused?
options: The overhead camshaft base circle will wear flat within 500 miles
The intake valve will fail to open to full lift when idling cold
Engine oil consumption will double past the positive valve stem seal
The thin feather-edge margin will overheat, causing pre-ignition and burning
rationale: The valve margin provides thermal mass around the perimeter of the valve head. If the margin is ground thinner than specification ("pie-crust" or feather edge), it cannot dissipate combustion heat rapidly enough, causing glowing hot spots (pre-ignition) and rapid valve burning.

question: Technician A says that exhaust valve seats are typically cut slightly wider than intake valve seats to improve heat transfer from the hot exhaust valve head into the water-cooled cylinder head casting. Technician B says that an overly narrow exhaust valve seat provides better heat dissipation than a wider seat. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Over 75% of the heat absorbed by an exhaust valve head is transferred out through the valve seat while the valve is closed. Therefore, exhaust valve seats are wider than intake seats to provide greater surface area for heat transfer.

question: While measuring valve stem-to-guide clearance on a disassembled cylinder head, a technician uses an outside micrometer to measure the valve stem diameter at three locations and uses a small-hole (split-ball) gauge coupled with an outside micrometer to measure the inside diameter of the valve guide. Which other tool setup is commonly specified by manufacturers to check valve guide wear quickly?
options: A dial indicator mounted against the slightly opened valve margin while rocking it
A strip of green Plastigage inserted lengthwise along the valve stem inside the guide bore
A telescoping gauge placed horizontally between the outer coils of the valve spring
A flat feeler gauge blade slid between the tapered valve keeper grooves and retainer
rationale: The two standard methods for measuring valve guide wear are: (1) direct measurement using a small-hole gauge and outside micrometer, and (2) the dial indicator "rock/wobble" method with the valve lifted slightly off its seat. (Note: the dial indicator wobble reading is usually about double the actual radial stem-to-guide clearance depending on manufacturer service geometry).

question: Because aluminum is too soft to withstand direct valve hammering, aluminum cylinder heads use pressed-in hardened sintered-alloy valve seat inserts. When replacing a damaged exhaust valve seat insert in an aluminum cylinder head, what is the standard machine-shop procedure to ensure proper interference fit without galling the aluminum counterbore?
options: Machine the aluminum counterbore 0.015 in. larger than the seat insert and glue the insert in place with high-temperature RTV silicone
Machine a 0.002–0.004 in. interference fit, chill the insert, warm the head, and drive it bottomed
Braze the steel valve seat insert directly to the aluminum casting using an oxy-acetylene welding torch
Hammer the new seat insert cold into the unmachined bore using a ball-peen hammer and stake the combustion chamber with a cold chisel
rationale: Valve seat inserts in aluminum cylinder heads rely on a precise radial interference fit (typically 0.002 to 0.004 in.) and full bottom contact with the counterbore floor to transfer heat out of the valve. Chilling the new seat insert in dry ice or liquid nitrogen shrinks the insert while gently warming the aluminum head expands the counterbore, allowing the insert to drop/seat cleanly to the bottom without tearing aluminum from the bore wall.

question: An overhead-valve (OHV) pushrod engine has a loud clattering noise from Cylinder #3. Upon removing the valve cover and pushrod, the technician discovers the bottom of the hydraulic flat-tappet lifter is worn concave (dished inward). What MUST be done to repair this engine properly?
options: Install a single new hydraulic lifter in the Cylinder #3 bore and reuse the existing camshaft
Grind the tip of the pushrod flat to match the lifter
Shim the rocker arm pedestal on Cylinder #3 by 0.060 in.
Replace the camshaft and all flat lifters, and apply break-in lube to all lobes
rationale: Healthy flat-tappet lifters have a slightly convex (crowned) bottom surface so that contact with the slightly tapered camshaft lobe causes the lifter to rotate in its bore. Once a lifter bottom wears concave, its mating camshaft lobe is also worn round/flat. Installing a new lifter on a worn cam lobe (or vice versa) will destroy the new part within minutes; both the camshaft and lifters must be replaced together.

question: How do you accurately calculate camshaft lobe lift using an outside micrometer when the camshaft is removed from the engine?
options: Measure the base circle diameter and multiply by the rocker arm ratio
Subtract the base circle diameter (minor) from the nose-to-heel height (major)
Add the nose-to-heel height to the base circle diameter and divide by two
Measure the width of the camshaft lobe across the thrust face
rationale: Camshaft lobe lift is the difference between the maximum height of the lobe (measured from the tip of the nose to the heel) and the base circle diameter (measured 90 degrees across the round side of the lobe). Total valve lift equals lobe lift multiplied by the rocker arm ratio.

question: An engine with Variable Valve Timing (VVT) sets Diagnostic Trouble Code (DTC) P0011 ("A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance Bank 1) and idles roughly after an overdue oil change. All of the following could cause this condition EXCEPT:
options: A clogged mesh filter screen on the VVT Oil Control Valve (OCV) solenoid
Sludge sticking the spool valve inside the VVT Oil Control Valve
Using engine oil with a viscosity dramatically heavier than manufacturer specifications
A leaking rear main crankshaft oil seal
rationale: Hydraulic VVT cam phasers rely on clean, properly pressurized engine oil metered through a pulse-width-modulated Oil Control Valve (OCV) solenoid. Sludge, clogged OCV screens, or improper oil viscosity directly impede phaser movement, whereas a minor external rear main seal seep does not cause a cam phaser to stick over-advanced.

question: A technician is adjusting mechanical (solid) valve lash on an overhead-cam engine that uses replaceable steel adjusting shims atop the bucket tappets. On Cylinder #2 intake, the measured cold valve clearance is 0.10 mm (0.004 in.), while the factory specification is 0.25 mm ± 0.03 mm (0.010 in.). Upon removing the existing shim, the technician measures its thickness with a micrometer at 2.80 mm. What thickness replacement shim must be installed to set the clearance exactly at 0.25 mm?
rationale: Formula: New Shim Thickness = Old Shim Thickness + (Measured Clearance - Specified Clearance). Here, the measured clearance (0.10 mm) is 0.15 mm TOO TIGHT compared to the 0.25 mm target. To increase the gap by 0.15 mm, you must install a shim that is 0.15 mm THINNER than the existing 2.80 mm shim: 2.80 mm - 0.15 mm = 2.65 mm.

question: What is the mechanical difference between an "interference" engine and a "non-interference" (free-wheeling) engine if the timing belt breaks while the engine is running?
options: In an interference engine, the connecting rod beams strike the bottom of the cylinder block skirt
In an interference engine, the intake and exhaust camshaft lobes collide with each other
In a non-interference engine, the internal oil pump stops turning if the serpentine belt snaps
In an interference engine, open valves extend into the piston's TDC path and bend if timing fails
rationale: An interference engine has high compression and deep valve lift such that the path of an open valve extends below the top deck reached by the piston at TDC. If the timing belt snaps or jumps significantly, the ascending pistons collide with the stationary open valves, bending the valve stems or fracturing guides/pistons.

question: Technician A says that positive-type valve stem seals grip only the upper valve stem tip and ride up and down with the valve without touching the valve guide boss. Technician B says that umbrella-type (deflector) valve stem seals move up and down with the valve stem and act like a shield to deflect oil spray away from the guide opening. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Technician B is correct: umbrella (deflector) seals grip the valve stem and move up and down with the valve to shield the guide opening from oil splash. Technician A is incorrect: positive-type valve stem seals press stationary onto the machined top boss of the valve guide and wipe/meter oil off the valve stem as it slides through the seal.

question: When inspecting tubular pushrods removed from an OHV V8 engine, what is a simple, reliable way to check whether any of the pushrods are slightly bent?
options: Measure the overall end-to-end length of each pushrod with a steel tape measure
Roll each pushrod across a flat surface plate and look for wobble or a changing gap
Tap each pushrod against the cast-iron workbench and compare the acoustic ring pitch
Magnetize the aluminum pushrod with a yoke and sprinkle dry iron powder over it
rationale: Rolling a pushrod on a flat surface plate (or checking it in V-blocks with a dial indicator) immediately reveals any bend as the center of the rod lifts and drops against the flat surface. Additionally, technicians should always blow compressed air through hollow pushrods to verify the internal oil passage is clear.

question: During a timing chain replacement on a DOHC V6 engine, the technician notices that the new timing chain has three brightly colored links (two copper links and one dark blue link). What is the purpose of these colored links?
options: They mark the chain links that align with the cam and crank sprocket dots
They identify the removable master link pin that must be driven out to separate the chain
They indicate which chain links contain solid graphite self-lubricating roller bushings
They are guaranteed to realign with the sprocket dots after every two crankshaft revolutions
rationale: Colored links (plated links) on OEM and replacement timing chains are alignment markers placed at exact link intervals to match the timing dimples/marks on the camshaft phasers and crankshaft sprocket during initial assembly. (Note: Choice D is a common shop myth—once you rotate the crankshaft two turns after installation, the camshaft marks will align with the housing marks again, but the colored chain links usually take dozens of revolutions to line back up with the sprocket dots!).

question: A technician is performing a dye penetrant inspection to check a cast-aluminum cylinder head for suspected hairline cracks between the valve seats. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: Connect an electromagnetic yoke across the aluminum head and dust iron filings over the seats
Spray white developer powder first, apply red penetrant dye over it, and heat with a propane torch
Clean the head, apply red penetrant, wipe excess dye, and spray white developer
Submerge the uncleaned cylinder head in diesel fuel and inspect under polarized shop lights
rationale: Because aluminum is non-magnetic, magnetic particle inspection (flux/iron powder) cannot be used. Dye penetrant testing works on aluminum and cast iron by cleaning the part, applying penetrant dye (which seeps into cracks via capillary action), wiping the surface clean, and spraying white developer, which draws the red dye out of the crack into a visible crimson line.

question: When installing a new hydraulic timing belt or timing chain tensioner that comes retained by a steel locking pin (grenade pin), when should the locking pin be pulled out?
options: Before bolting the hydraulic tensioner housing onto the engine block
After starting the engine and warming the coolant to full operating temperature
While an assistant cranks the engine over with the starter motor engaged
Only after routing the drive, putting slack on the tensioner side, and checking marks
rationale: The locking pin holds the hydraulic plunger compressed for installation. Pulling the pin before routing the belt/chain makes installation impossible (and requires slowly compressing the plunger in a vise to reset it). It must be pulled only after the belt/chain is installed with all slack positioned on the tensioner side and timing marks verified.

question: A DOHC V6 engine stalls immediately when coming to a stop after highway cruising, sets DTC P0012 ("A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Retarded Bank 1), and rattles loudly for two seconds on cold startup. Using a bidirectional scan tool at hot idle, the technician commands the Bank 1 intake VVT Oil Control Valve (OCV) from 0% to 80% duty cycle and observes the engine immediately stumble and stall, returning smoothly to idle only when duty cycle is returned to 0% and the accelerator is blipped. However, when the engine returns to hot idle after driving, actual camshaft timing occasionally hangs 18 degrees advanced and fails to lock at the base park position. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A sheared internal phaser locking pin with rotor vane oil bypass leakage
An electrically open VVT Oil Control Valve solenoid winding on Bank 1
A primary timing chain installed three teeth retarded on the crankshaft sprocket
A shorted camshaft position (CMP) Hall-effect sensor reference wire
rationale: Because commanding the OCV with a scan tool actively moves the cam timing and stalls the engine, the OCV coil and hydraulic supply circuit are functional, ruling out an open solenoid (B). A sheared or sticking phaser locking pin prevents the rotor from mechanically locking into its base timing position when oil pressure drops at idle or shutdown, causing startup rattle and allowing the cam to drift or hang out of position. A chain jumped by three teeth (C) would cause a permanent correlation code and constant misfire rather than an intermittent return-to-idle fault, and a shorted CMP wire (D) would set a circuit low/high code rather than a mechanical phase problem.

question: An overhead-cam engine exhibits a rough idle, slow cranking cadence, and sets both DTC P0016 (Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation Bank 1 Sensor A) and DTC P0017 (Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation Bank 1 Sensor B) simultaneously. Neither cam phaser responds abnormally when commanded individually, as both the intake and exhaust camshafts on Bank 1 read uniformly 9 degrees retarded relative to the crankshaft on a dual-trace lab scope. What is the MOST likely cause of these two fault codes occurring together?
options: Both intake and exhaust VVT Oil Control Valves failed simultaneously in full advance
A stretched primary timing chain, worn plastic guides, or an over-extended tensioner
A contaminated mass airflow (MAF) sensor hot wire under-reporting intake air mass
Excessively tight mechanical bucket tappet valve lash on Cylinder #1
rationale: When both the intake (P0016) and exhaust (P0017) camshafts on the same bank shift equally in the retarded direction relative to the crankshaft, the mechanical link common to both camshafts—the primary timing chain and its guide/tensioner system—has elongated or worn. As the chain stretches and plastic guides wear down, the distance along the tension side increases, retarding both camshafts together even as the ratcheting tensioner clicks out to its limit. Simultaneous OCV failure in the exact same degree offset (A) is highly improbable, and MAF sensors (C) or valve lash (D) do not alter the phase relationship between the CKP and CMP tone wheels.

question: After completing a three-angle valve job on a cylinder head, the technician measures the valve spring installed height on Cylinder #4 intake at 1.835 in. using a telescoping spring height micrometer. The service manual specifies an installed height of 1.780 in. to 1.790 in. Which combination of calibrated valve spring shims should be placed beneath the spring to bring the installed height within specification?
options: One 0.030 in. shim and one 0.015 in. shim (total 0.045 in.)
One 0.060 in. shim and one 0.030 in. shim (total 0.090 in.)
One 0.015 in. shim only
No shims are needed; grind 0.050 in. off the top of the valve spring
rationale: Subtracting the desired installed height range (1.780 in. to 1.790 in.) from the measured height (1.835 in.) shows that the spring pocket needs between 0.045 in. and 0.055 in. of shim thickness (1.835 - 0.045 = 1.790 in.). Stacking one 0.030 in. shim and one 0.015 in. shim provides 0.045 in., bringing the installed height to 1.790 in., right inside the factory window. Using 0.090 in. of shims (B) would reduce the height to 1.745 in. and risk coil bind, while 0.015 in. (C) leaves the height too tall at 1.820 in..

question: Technician A says that when testing open valve spring pressure on a bench spring tester, the spring is measured at its uncompressed free standing height. Technician B says that at full valve lift, the adjacent coils of a valve spring should touch solidly against each other (0.000 in. clearance) to stop the valve from opening too far. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Neither technician is correct. Open valve spring pressure is measured by compressing the spring to a height equal to its installed height minus maximum valve lift (not its uncompressed free height). Furthermore, when the valve is at full lift, there must still be at least 0.060 in. (1.5 mm) of clearance remaining between coils; if the coils touch solidly ('coil bind'), valvetrain components will bend or snap immediately.

question: A technician is calculating exhaust valve stem-to-guide clearance on a disassembled cylinder head. Using an outside micrometer, the exhaust valve stem measures 0.3412 in. inside the guide contact area. Using a split-ball small-hole gauge and the same outside micrometer, the inside diameter of the exhaust valve guide measures 0.3458 in. near the top and bottom of the guide. If the maximum allowable exhaust stem-to-guide service clearance is 0.0035 in., what is the measured clearance and what does it indicate?
options: 0.0023 in.; the valve guide clearance is well within factory limits
0.0046 in.; guide clearance is excessive and requires guide service
0.6870 in.; the technician used the wrong measurement scale
0.0011 in.; the valve stem is seized in the guide
rationale: Valve stem-to-guide clearance is calculated by subtracting the valve stem outside diameter from the valve guide inside diameter: 0.3458 in. - 0.3412 in. = 0.0046 in.. Because 0.0046 in. exceeds the 0.0035 in. service limit by 0.0011 in., the guide is excessively worn ("bell-mouthed") and will cause high oil consumption, poor valve seat concentricity, and burned exhaust valves if not repaired.

question: Three methods for restoring excessive valve stem-to-guide clearance in an integral cast-iron cylinder head are being discussed: knurling the existing guide, reaming the guide to accept a valve with an oversize stem, and machining the guide bore to install a thin-wall phosphor-bronze guide liner insert. All of the following statements about these repair methods are true EXCEPT:
options: After installing new valve guides or bronze liners, the valve seats do not need to be re-cut or checked for concentricity
Reaming the integral guide enlarges its inside diameter so a new replacement valve with an oversize stem (+0.003 in., +0.005 in., or +0.015 in.) can restore proper clearance
Installing bronze guide inserts provides superior lubricity, heat transfer, and wear resistance compared to knurling
Guide knurling uses an arbor to displace metal inward into raised spiral ridges and is only viable when existing guide wear is slight (typically less than 0.006 in.)
rationale: Whenever a valve guide is reamed, knurled, replaced, or fitted with a bronze liner, the centerline axis of the guide shifts slightly. Therefore, you MUST always machine or grind the valve seat after completing valve guide work so the seat is perfectly concentric with the new guide centerline; skipping seat machining (A) guarantees an off-center, leaking valve. All three other statements accurately describe standard machine shop guide restoration procedures.

question: A technician mounts a valve seat runout dial indicator onto a tapered pilot inserted snugly into the valve guide. When rotating the indicator sleeve 360 degrees around the freshly cut 45-degree valve seat, what is the maximum acceptable valve seat concentricity (total indicator runout) for a precision engine rebuild?
options: 0.002 in. (0.05 mm) or less
rationale: Valve seat concentricity (runout relative to the valve guide axis) must be within 0.001 in. to 0.002 in. (0.025 to 0.05 mm) total indicator reading (TIR) to ensure the valve seals tightly around its entire 360-degree circumference on initial seating. Any runout approaching 0.015 in. to 0.060 in. (A, B, D) would leave a wide gap on one side of the seat, causing compression leakage and immediate valve face burning.

question: Technician A says that an "interference angle" in a valve job is created by grinding the valve face at a 44-degree angle and the cylinder head valve seat at a 45-degree angle, resulting in a 1-degree hairline contact edge that seals rapidly during initial engine break-in. Technician B says that when a manufacturer specifies an interference angle, the valve and seat should be heavily hand-lapped with coarse silicon-carbide lapping compound until a 0.100 in. wide gray matte band is formed before assembly. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Technician A is correct: grinding the valve face 0.5° to 1.0° shallower (44°) than the seat (45°) produces an interference angle that concentrates spring pressure on the outer top edge of the seat to break through carbon deposits and seat instantly upon start-up. Technician B is incorrect: lapping an interference-angle valve job with abrasive compound grinds away the 1-degree differential and leaves abrasive grit embedded in the seat metal, defeating the entire purpose of the interference angle.

question: While performing a three-angle valve job on a cylinder head with 45-degree seats, the technician performs a Prussian Blue check and observes that the 45-degree seat contact ring is 0.085 in. wide (intake specification is 0.045–0.060 in.) and sits too high on the valve face, dangerously close to the outer margin. Which stone or cutter angle must the technician use to narrow the seat AND move the contact ring downward toward the valve stem?
options: The 45-degree primary seat cutter/stone
The 60-degree bottom throat cutter/stone
The 30-degree top narrowing cutter/stone
A 90-degree flat facing stone
rationale: Because the contact band is too wide and positioned too high toward the valve margin, removing metal from the top (combustion chamber side) of the 45° seat using a 30° top-cut stone narrows the 45° seat from the top edge down, simultaneously lowering the contact ring toward the center of the valve face. Using a 60° throat cut (B) would narrow the seat from the bottom and push the contact ring even higher onto the margin, while cutting more with the 45° stone (A) only makes the seat wider.

question: An overhead-cam (OHC) engine equipped with solid mechanical bucket tappets (no hydraulic lifters) has its valve seats and valve faces ground during a cylinder head overhaul. No shims are changed during initial test assembly on the bench. How will grinding the valves and seats affect the cold mechanical valve lash (clearance between the cam base circle and bucket tappet)?
options: Camshaft lobe lift will increase by 0.025 in.
Valve lash will increase (become looser), causing loud valvetrain clatter
Valve lash will remain completely unaffected by valve seat grinding
Valve lash will decrease (tighten), holding the valves slightly open hot
rationale: Grinding metal from the valve face and valve seat causes the valve to recede ("sink") deeper into the cylinder head casting toward the camshaft. This moves the tip of the valve stem closer to the camshaft base circle, reducing (tightening) the mechanical clearance between the bucket tappet and the camshaft lobe. If thinner shims are not installed (or the valve stem tip is not ground within limits), the tight lash can hold the valve off its seat as the stem expands thermally, burning the valve.

question: What is the effect of excessive valve seat recession (a sunken valve from repeated seat grinding) on an OHV pushrod engine with non-adjustable pedestal-mount rocker arms and hydraulic lifters?
options: The stamped-steel rocker arm geometric lever ratio increases from 1.5:1 to 2.0:1
The pushrod becomes effectively too short to reach the lifter socket and falls out from under the rocker arm
The higher stem tip pushes the pushrod down, bottoming the lifter plunger
Main oil gallery pressure increases by 15 psi due to restricted flow through the pushrod
rationale: When a valve sinks deeper into the seat, the stem tip rises higher toward the rocker arm. On a non-adjustable hydraulic valvetrain, this increased stem height pushes the rocker arm tip up and drives the pushrod end down, compressing the hydraulic lifter plunger further into its body (excessive lifter preload). If the plunger bottoms out against the bottom of the lifter body, the lifter acts like a solid link that is too long, holding the valve off its seat and causing a loss of compression.

question: A technician is performing a bench leak-down rate test on a hydraulic lash adjuster (HLA) submerged in a cup of clean test fluid (mineral spirits or kerosene) using a weighted fixture that applies a specified load (e.g., 50 lbs) after the adjuster is bled of air. All of the following indicate a defective hydraulic lash adjuster EXCEPT:
options: The plunger collapses instantaneously to the bottom as soon as weight is applied, even after repeated bleeding attempts
The plunger drops 0.100 in. evenly in 15–45 seconds under the test load
The plunger is seized solid and will not compress at all after sitting under load for several minutes
The outer body of the lash adjuster shows heavy galling and deep vertical scoring
rationale: Hydraulic lifters/lash adjusters are engineered with a controlled micro-clearance between the precision plunger and body so they leak down at a slow, calibrated rate (typically 10 to 60 seconds for a given stroke in test fluid) to compensate for thermal expansion of the valve stem. Instantaneous collapse (A) indicates a leaking internal check ball or worn plunger, seizure (C) indicates varnish/debris lockup, and body scoring (D) requires replacement.

question: When servicing bucket-style or pivot-style hydraulic lash adjusters (HLAs) prior to installation, Technician A says HLAs should be soaked in solvent or gasoline to wash all oil out of the internal high-pressure chamber so they install completely dry. Technician B says that if an HLA is pumped up rock-solid with thick grease before installation, it can hold a valve slightly open during initial cranking and cause low compression until the adjuster bleeds down. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Technician B is correct: over-extending an HLA or packing it with heavy grease prevents the plunger from bleeding down to its operating height when the cam base circle rotates around, holding the valves open ('lifter pump-up') and causing zero compression during initial cranking. Technician A is incorrect: HLAs must be bled and primed in clean engine oil, never installed bone-dry with solvent inside.

question: A V6 engine with roller finger followers and overhead camshafts develops a loud, rhythmic metallic ticking noise from the right bank valve cover and sets a Cylinder #2 misfire code (P0302). Upon removing the valve cover, the technician finds fine steel needle bearings scattered in the cylinder head oil return puddle and deep grooves worn into the Cylinder #2 intake camshaft lobe. What happened?
options: The intake valve spring was installed with the damper coils upside down
The port fuel injector pintle tip broke off and dropped into the crankcase
The roller follower bearing failed, letting the locked roller skid on the lobe
The spark plug ground electrode gap was set 0.005 in. wider than specification
rationale: Roller finger followers (rocker arms) pivot on a hydraulic lash adjuster at one end, rest on the valve stem at the other, and use a needle-bearing roller in the center to follow the camshaft lobe. When low oil flow or metal fatigue causes the roller's tiny needle bearings to fail, the roller stops turning and skids against the cam lobe, rapidly grinding down the hardened cam lobe nose (reducing valve lift and causing a dead cylinder misfire) while shedding needle bearings into the head.

question: After milling an OHV engine block deck and resurfacing the cylinder heads, a technician checks rocker arm-to-valve tip geometry on Cylinder #1 by painting the valve stem tip with layout dye, installing an adjustable pushrod checking tool, and rotating the crankshaft through two revolutions. The wiped witness mark on the valve stem tip is narrow and centered across the middle third of the valve stem tip. What does this contact pattern indicate?
options: The threaded rocker arm stud is bent at a 15-degree angle toward the intake port
The checking pushrod is 0.150 in. too long, pushing the sweep pattern off the exhaust edge
The checking pushrod length is correct, giving centered geometry and low side-load
The checking pushrod is 0.150 in. too short, pulling the sweep pattern onto the intake edge
rationale: Proper rocker arm geometry requires the rocker tip (or roller tip) to sweep across the center of the valve stem tip in a narrow band during full valve lift. If the pushrod is too long or too short after block/head milling, the contact patch shifts toward the inboard or outboard edge of the valve tip, applying destructive lateral side-load that rapidly wears out the valve guides and stem tips.

question: A technician is checking camshaft straightness (bend/runout) before installing a long OHC camshaft into an aluminum cylinder head. The technician rests the #1 and #5 outer camshaft journals on precision V-blocks on a surface plate and positions a dial indicator plunger vertically against the #3 center main journal. While rotating the camshaft one full turn, the dial indicator needle sweeps from 0.000 in. to 0.0045 in.. If the maximum allowable camshaft runout specification is 0.0015 in., what will happen if this camshaft is installed?
options: The bent camshaft will bind inside the cam tunnel bores, causing galling or breakage
The camshaft will straighten itself permanently once the cam bearing caps are torqued down
Only the cold mechanical valve lash on Cylinder #1 will be affected by the bend
Main gallery oil pressure will rise by 20 psi due to reduced cam journal clearance
rationale: Overhead camshafts run directly in precision-machined aluminum bores in the cylinder head (often without replaceable bearing inserts) with only 0.0015 to 0.0030 in. of oil clearance. A camshaft with 0.0045 in. of bend/runout exceeds the oil clearance film and will bind heavily when the cam caps are torqued, scraping the aluminum bores, seizing the camshaft, and snapping the timing belt or chain.

question: When measuring camshaft journal oil clearance on an OHC cylinder head that uses removable cam bearing caps, Technician A says you can remove the valve followers/lifters so valve spring pressure does not push against the cam lobes, lay strips of green Plastigage across the cam journals, torque the cam caps in sequence to specification, and remove the caps to measure the crushed Plastigage width. Technician B says that if the camshaft rotates tightly by hand after lubricating the journals and torquing the caps (with followers removed), the cylinder head cam tunnel alignment should be checked for warpage with an arbor/straightedge or bore gauge. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Both technicians are correct. Removing the followers/tappets is mandatory when checking OHC journal clearance with Plastigage; otherwise, the valve springs push the camshaft forcefully against the upper cap halves and give a false zero-clearance reading on top and huge clearance on the bottom (Technician A). Furthermore, whenever an aluminum OHC head overheats and warps on the bottom deck, the top camshaft tunnel also bows into a banana shape, binding the camshaft even if the bottom deck is later milled flat (Technician B).

question: On a belt-driven or chain-driven Single Overhead Cam (SOHC) engine where the crankshaft sprocket is in the block and the camshaft sprocket is in the cylinder head, resurfacing (milling) 0.015 in. (0.38 mm) of metal from the warped cylinder head deck moves the camshaft sprocket 0.015 in. closer to the crankshaft centerline. How does this dimensional change affect the engine?
options: It has zero effect on either the static compression ratio or camshaft valve timing
It decreases the static compression ratio and advances camshaft timing by 10 degrees
It increases effective cylinder bore diameter and lowers hot-idle oil pressure
It slightly raises the compression ratio and slightly retards camshaft valve timing
rationale: Milling the cylinder head deck reduces the volume of the combustion chamber domes (Vc), which directly increases the static compression ratio. In addition, moving the cylinder head closer to the crankshaft shortens the center-to-center distance between the crank and cam sprockets; when the tensioner takes up the slack on the slack side of the belt/chain, the camshaft rotates slightly backward against the direction of rotation, retarding valve timing.

question: A cast-iron cylinder head is suspected of having a crack in the exhaust port water jacket after a severe overheating episode. All of the following inspection methods are effective for locating cracks in a cast-iron cylinder head EXCEPT:
options: Magnetic particle inspection (Magnaflux) using an electromagnetic yoke and iron oxide powder
Pressure testing the cylinder head by bolting a block-off plate over the deck, pressurizing the water jacket with 30 psi of compressed air, and submerging the head in a heated water tank
Checking the cylinder head with an eddy-current non-ferrous anodized film thickness gauge
Liquid dye penetrant testing (red penetrant and white developer)
rationale: Cast iron is ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle testing (A) works exceptionally well on surface cracks, pressure testing in a hot tank (B) reveals internal port/water-jacket cracks that open under thermal expansion, and dye penetrant (D) works on any clean non-porous metal surface. An eddy-current anodized film thickness gauge (C) is a paint/coating thickness tool for aluminum body panels and cannot detect cracks in cast iron.

question: During a cylinder head rebuild, a technician inspects a set of hollow, sodium-filled exhaust valves removed from a turbocharged engine. Which safety and service precaution applies specifically to sodium-filled valves?
options: Hollow sodium-filled valves run hotter than solid valves and cannot be used with bronze guides
Never cut open a sodium-filled valve stem or expose the internal metallic sodium to water
Hollow sodium-filled valve heads must be drilled open to drain the sodium before refacing
Bent sodium-filled valve stems up to 0.030 in. runout should be straightened in a shop press
rationale: Hollow sodium-filled exhaust valves contain elemental metallic sodium sealed inside the stem. At operating temperature (above 208°F / 98°C), the sodium melts into a liquid that sloshes up and down as the valve moves, transferring heat rapidly from the hot valve head up into the water-cooled valve guide. If a hollow stem is cut open or fractured and exposed to water or skin moisture, elemental sodium reacts exothermically, liberating hydrogen gas and igniting explosively.

question: A technician is diagnosing a persistent DTC P0018 (Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation Bank 2 Sensor A) on a 60-degree DOHC V6 engine that just had its cylinder heads reinstalled by another shop. Only Bank 2 intake cam correlation is flagged; Bank 1 intake/exhaust and Bank 2 exhaust are all at 0 degrees error. When the technician pulls the Bank 2 valve cover, both colored timing chain links appear properly aligned with the sprocket dots, and the chain tensioner is tight. What is the MOST likely cause of DTC P0018?
options: The Bank 1 exhaust VVT Oil Control Valve electrical connector was left unplugged
The primary crankshaft timing sprocket woodruff keyway sheared completely off the crank snout
The crankcase was filled with 5W-30 conventional motor oil instead of 0W-20 synthetic oil
The rear CMP reluctor wheel slipped on the cam or the phaser dowel pin sheared
rationale: Because only a single camshaft (Bank 2 intake) shows a permanent correlation fault while the timing marks on the front of the phaser match the chain links and all other three camshafts are in time, the mechanical phase shift is isolated between that single phaser's sprocket teeth and the CMP sensor tone ring at the rear of the camshaft. Either the phaser's alignment dowel pin sheared/missed its slot during installation, or the pressed-on reluctor wheel slipped on the camshaft tube. A sheared crank keyway (B) would throw all four camshafts out of correlation.

question: When inspecting variable-rate (progressive-pitch) or conical beehive valve springs prior to installation on a cylinder head, how should the tightly wound (closer-spaced) coils of a progressive-pitch spring be oriented?
options: With the closely wound coils facing up against the moving valve spring retainer
Alternating every other valve with the tight coils up on intakes and down on exhausts
With the closely wound coils facing down against the stationary head seat
Progressive-pitch springs must only be installed horizontally
rationale: The closely spaced ("damping") coils of a progressive-pitch valve spring represent the heaviest concentration of wire mass. Installing the closely wound end downward against the stationary cylinder head spring pocket minimizes the reciprocating mass that must accelerate up and down with the valve retainer, reducing valvetrain inertia and raises the RPM threshold where valve float occurs.

question: A technician measures camshaft axial end play on a pushrod V8 engine that uses a bolt-on camshaft thrust plate behind the camshaft sprocket. Using a dial indicator mounted with its plunger parallel to the camshaft centerline, the technician pries the camshaft fully rearward and forward and reads 0.016 in. of end play (specification is 0.002 to 0.006 in.). What causes this condition, and why must it be corrected?
options: Worn valve stem oil seals; it allows pressurized coolant into the intake manifold runners
Over-torqued rocker arm pedestal bolts; it causes the gerotor oil pump to cavitate
Excessive crankshaft main bearing oil clearance; it bends the connecting rod beams at idle
A worn camshaft thrust plate; axial walk alters timing and lets lifters walk off
rationale: Camshaft end play is controlled by the camshaft thrust plate (or thrust button/flange) sandwiched between the front camshaft journal shoulder and the rear hub of the camshaft sprocket. Because helical distributor gears, oil pump drive gears, or tapered flat-tappet lobes exert fore-and-aft axial thrust on the camshaft, 0.016 in. of end play lets the camshaft walk back and forth, causing erratic cam sensor/ignition timing and allowing flat-tappet lifters to strike the adjacent lobes.

question: After reconditioning a set of valves on a wet-stone valve refacer machine, the technician notices faint chatter marks (ripples) around the newly ground 45-degree valve face. All of the following machine shop issues can cause valve refacer chatter marks EXCEPT:
options: A glazed or out-of-round grinding wheel that needs to be trued with the diamond dresser
Grinding an uncleaned valve stem in a dirty chuck collet or extending the valve head too far out from the collet
Feeding the valve across the grinding wheel too aggressively without wrapping up with slow spark-out passes
Using fresh, clean water-soluble grinding coolant flowing steadily over the stone
rationale: Steady flow of clean grinding coolant (D) cools the valve head, flushes away swarf, and promotes a mirror-smooth finish. Chatter marks on a valve face are caused by mechanical vibration or wheel loading—specifically a glazed/untrued grinding wheel (A), excessive valve stem overhang or carbon on the stem causing chuck runout (B), or taking heavy cuts without letting the stone "spark out" (C).

question: Technician A says that when checking a multi-valve aluminum cylinder head for warpage, you must also measure the flatness of the intake and exhaust manifold mounting flange surfaces using a straightedge and feeler gauge. Technician B says that if an overhead-cam aluminum cylinder head is warped 0.018 in. (maximum resurface limit is 0.008 in.), heating and straightening the head in a specialized oven jig before light skim-milling is preferred over milling 0.018 in. directly off the deck because heavy milling leaves the camshaft tunnel bowed and the chambers unequal. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Both technicians are correct. Overheating warps not only the head gasket surface but also the manifold flanges (which can cause exhaust leaks or cracked manifolds if not checked, per Technician A) and the overhead camshaft bore line. If a banana-warped OHC aluminum head is simply milled 0.018 in. flat on the bottom without thermally straightening the casting first (Technician B), the camshaft tunnel remains bowed—binding the camshaft—and the end combustion chambers end up with much smaller volumes than the center chambers.

question: Before using a dial bore gauge to measure cylinder bore wear on an engine block with a standard bore specification of 3.5000 in., how should the technician set up and zero the dial bore gauge?
options: Insert the dial bore gauge into the very top worn ring ridge of Cylinder #1 and zero the bezel at that position
Zero the dial bore gauge inside an outside micrometer locked at 3.5000 in. while rocking for the minimum reading
Compress the dial bore gauge plunger fully by hand against a flat surface plate and set the dial bezel to zero
Zero the dial bore gauge inside an old piston skirt before inserting it into the cylinder bore
rationale: A dial bore gauge is a comparative measuring instrument that must first be calibrated to the nominal standard bore specification (3.5000 in.) using a precision setting fixture or a locked outside micrometer. Rocking the bore gauge between the micrometer anvils locates the true perpendicular diameter (the minimum reversal point of the needle), where the bezel is zeroed so any bore reading directly displays wear in ten-thousandths of an inch above 3.5000 in.

question: While inspecting an engine block with a dial bore gauge, a technician measures the top of Cylinder #2 perpendicular to the crankshaft centerline (thrust-to-thrust) at 3.5035 in., and parallel to the crankshaft centerline (front-to-back) at the exact same depth at 3.5010 in. What does the 0.0025 in. difference between these two measurements represent?
options: Piston-to-wall clearance
Cylinder bore taper
Cylinder bore out-of-round (ovality)
Deck surface distortion
rationale: Out-of-round (ovality) is the difference between the cylinder diameter measured perpendicular to the crankshaft (thrust direction) and parallel to the crankshaft (pin direction) at the same depth in the bore.

question: Before pushing a piston and connecting rod assembly upward out of the top of a high-mileage cast-iron engine block, a technician finds a pronounced unworn metal step (ring ridge) at the very top of the cylinder bore. What will likely happen if the piston is forced out past a heavy ring ridge without using a ridge reamer first?
options: The crankshaft connecting rod journal will become deeply scored on the bottom
The top compression ring will strike the ridge and break the piston ring lands
The connecting rod cap bolts will stretch permanently past their yield point
The cast-iron cylinder block top deck surface will warp out of flat
rationale: If a piston with carbon-packed ring grooves is driven forcefully through an unreamed top cylinder ridge, the top compression ring catches on the step and slams downward against the second ring land, fracturing or bending the piston ring lands and ruining an otherwise reusable piston.

question: When deglazing (honing) cylinder walls during an engine re-ring job, the technician strokes the hone steadily up and down while rotating it to produce an intersecting crosshatch pattern. What is the ideal included crosshatch angle, and what is its purpose?
options: 0 degrees (purely horizontal rings); to scrape 100% of the oil off the cylinder walls
30 to 45 degrees (45–60° included); to retain oil for ring seating and lubrication
90 degrees (purely vertical scratches); to vent combustion blow-by gases into the oil pan
85 degrees (steep vertical crosshatch); to prevent the piston from rotating in the cylinder
rationale: A proper cylinder wall crosshatch pattern (typically a 22°–30° angle to the deck, forming a 45°–60° included intersection angle) holds a controlled microscopic film of oil to lubricate the rings while helping the new piston rings rotate and seat properly during break-in.

question: After honing an engine block, what is the recommended method for cleaning the cylinder bores to remove microscopic abrasive honing grit and metallic particles?
options: Wipe the cylinder bores once with a shop rag soaked in leaded gasoline and leave the walls dry
Scrub bores with hot soapy water and a brush until a white towel wipes clean, then oil
Blow the dry cylinder bores out using 120 psi compressed shop air and install pistons dry
Spray chlorinated brake cleaner down the cylinder bores and install the piston assemblies immediately
rationale: Petroleum solvents (like mineral spirits or brake cleaner) tend to redistribute silicon-carbide honing grit into the pores of cast iron rather than lifting it out. Scrubbing with hot detergent/soapy water floats the abrasive grit out of the crosshatch valleys; once a white lint-free towel wipes clean without gray residue, the bores are dried and immediately oiled to prevent flash rust.

question: Where on the piston should an outside micrometer be positioned to accurately measure piston diameter for calculating piston-to-wall clearance?
options: Diagonally from the top edge of the piston crown to the bottom edge of the skirt
Across the top compression ring land parallel to the wrist pin axis near the crown
Inside the hollow anodized wrist pin bosses using a telescoping bore gauge
Across the skirt perpendicular (90°) to the wrist pin at the specified height
rationale: Pistons are cam-ground (slightly elliptical when cold so they become round as the heavy pin bosses expand when hot) and tapered (smaller at the crown than at the skirt). Therefore, piston diameter is always measured across the skirt, perpendicular (90°) to the wrist pin axis.

question: A technician is checking the end gap of a new top compression ring before installing it onto the piston. How should the ring be positioned inside the cylinder bore prior to measuring the gap with a feeler gauge?
options: Install the ring into the piston groove first, then slide a feeler gauge between the ring and bore wall
Hold the bare ring at a 45-degree angle at the very top of the unreamed cylinder ridge
Push the bare ring squarely down into the bore using an inverted piston crown
Measure the uncompressed free gap while holding the ring loosely in your hands on the bench
rationale: Piston ring end gap must be measured with the ring pushed squarely into the cylinder bore (using an upside-down piston as a square pusher) to the lower/unworn portion of ring travel. If the ring is tilted even slightly, the measured gap will be inaccurate.

question: What happens during engine operation if a new top compression ring is installed with insufficient (too tight) ring end gap?
options: Crankcase blow-by pressure increases only during cold morning engine warm-up
Engine oil consumption decreases to zero and highway fuel economy improves by 15%
Thermal expansion makes the ring ends butt solidly, buckling and snapping the ring
Connecting rod big-end bearing oil clearance increases by 0.003 in. at high RPM
rationale: The top compression ring is exposed to intense combustion heat and expands in circumference. If the ring end gap is too small, the ring ends butt solidly against each other under load, forcing the ring to expand outward with tremendous radial force that scuffs/scores the cylinder wall and snaps the ring or ring land.

question: A technician is calculating piston-to-cylinder wall clearance on Cylinder #4 during an engine rebuild. Using an outside micrometer at the manufacturer's specified gauge point on the piston skirt (perpendicular to the wrist pin), the piston measures 3.8732 in. Using a dial bore gauge at the middle of Cylinder #4 along the thrust axis, the cylinder bore measures 3.8750 in. What is the piston-to-wall clearance, and is it typical for a cast-aluminum hypereutectic street piston?
options: 7.7482 in.; the two measurements must be added together rather than subtracted
0.0036 in.; no, the clearance is double the specification because radius was not divided by two
0.0018 in.; yes, this meets the 0.0010–0.0022 in. hypereutectic piston specification
0.0009 in.; the cylinder block must be bored 0.020 in. oversize immediately
rationale: Piston-to-cylinder wall clearance is calculated by subtracting the piston skirt diameter from the cylinder bore diameter: 3.8750 in. - 3.8732 in. = 0.0018 in. Because hypereutectic cast-aluminum pistons contain high silicon content (16%+) that reduces thermal expansion, they run tight piston-to-wall clearances of 0.0010 to 0.0022 in. (whereas forged 2618 racing pistons expand more and require 0.0035 to 0.0050 in.).

question: Most compression piston rings have a small dot, pip mark, or the word "TOP" stamped near the end gap on one flat surface. If this ring is accidentally installed upside down (with the dot facing down toward the oil pan), what is the MOST likely result?
options: High oil consumption because the inverted bevel scrapes oil UP into the chamber
The piston and ring assembly will refuse to slide through the ring compressor sleeve
Crankshaft thrust bearing axial end play will exceed maximum factory specifications
Pressurized engine coolant will seep past the ring pack into the lower oil pan
rationale: Directional compression/scraper rings have an inside bevel (torsional twist) or an outside tapered face designed to ride over the oil film on the upstroke and scrape oil down on the downstroke. Installing the ring upside down causes it to pump oil upward into the combustion chamber, resulting in severe oil consumption and blue smoke.

question: When installing three piston rings onto a piston, how should the ring end gaps be oriented relative to each other and the piston pin?
options: Positioned directly above the front and rear openings of the wrist pin bore
Aligned in a single straight vertical line down the major thrust face of the piston skirt
Staggered 120°–180° apart around the piston and away from the thrust and pin axes
Tack-welded closed with stainless filler wire after installing the rings into the grooves
rationale: Staggering the ring end gaps around the piston circumference creates a labyrinth path that prevents combustion gases from blowing straight down into the crankcase and prevents oil from migrating straight up into the chamber.

question: A technician is using green Plastigage (range 0.001–0.003 in.) to measure main bearing oil clearance on a crankshaft journal. All of the following rules must be followed for an accurate reading EXCEPT:
options: Rotate the crankshaft two full revolutions while the Plastigage is clamped inside the torqued bearing cap
Torque the main bearing cap bolts to full specification
Wipe all oil off the journal and bearing shell before laying the Plastigage strip across the journal width
Compare the width of the crushed Plastigage against the paper wrapper scale without removing it from the journal
rationale: You must NEVER rotate the crankshaft while Plastigage is clamped inside the bearing cap; rotating the shaft smears the wax strip around the journal and completely destroys the measurement. (Also note that when checking main bearings with the engine upright in the vehicle, the weight of the crankshaft must be supported so it does not artificially crush the lower cap Plastigage).

question: After torquing and removing a connecting rod cap during a Plastigage check, the crushed strip of Plastigage matches the 0.0015 in. (0.038 mm) bar at one side of the journal and the 0.0030 in. (0.076 mm) bar at the opposite side of the same journal. What does this tapered Plastigage width indicate?
options: The connecting rod bearing radial oil clearance is uniformly too tight across the journal
The crankshaft rod journal is tapered or the connecting rod big-end bore is distorted
The crankshaft main thrust bearing has excessive fore-and-aft axial end play
The journal exhibits normal hydrodynamic wear that requires no machining or service
rationale: If a strip of Plastigage laid across the width of a journal crushes wide at one end (0.0015 in.) and narrow at the other end (0.0030 in.), the journal (or housing bore) is tapered from side to side.

question: While rebuilding a bottom end, a technician notices that a crankshaft rod journal was machined (ground) 0.010 in. (0.25 mm) smaller than the factory standard diameter to remove scoring. What size connecting rod bearing inserts must be installed on this journal?
options: Standard size bearings with a 0.010 in. brass shim stock strip placed behind the steel back
0.010 in. undersize bearings (thicker shell walls to fit the 0.010 in. smaller journal)
0.010 in. oversize pistons paired with standard-thickness connecting rod bearings
Standard size bearings torqued 25 lb-ft tighter than the factory torque specification
rationale: In engine rebuilding terminology, bearings for a reground crankshaft are called undersize bearings (e.g., 0.010" U/S) because they are made to fit an undersized (smaller diameter) crankshaft journal by having a correspondingly thicker bearing wall. (Placing shims behind modern precision insert bearings is unacceptable as it ruins bearing crush and heat transfer).

question: What is the purpose of "bearing crush" (bearing spread and height slightly exceeding the housing bore split line before torquing the cap)?
options: To press the steel back tightly into the bore to stop spinning and aid heat transfer
To squeeze excess engine assembly lubricant out of the crankshaft cross-drilled oil holes
To allow the bearing inserts to rotate freely at half crankshaft speed inside the rod bore
To increase crankshaft axial thrust end play when the engine reaches operating temperature
rationale: Each bearing shell half is manufactured a few thousandths of an inch taller than an exact semicircle. When the cap bolts are torqued, this extra height ("crush") creates radial outward tension that locks the steel backing firmly into the housing bore for heat dissipation and prevents a "spun bearing."

question: When installing a crankshaft into an engine block that uses two separate flanged thrust bearing halves (one in the block saddle and one in the main bearing cap), what critical step must be performed just before torquing the thrust main bearing cap bolts to their final specification?
options: Insert a 0.015 in. feeler gauge blade permanently under the main bearing cap parting faces before tightening
Hammer the side of the main bearing cap with a steel sledgehammer after torquing the bolts to 100 lb-ft
Snug the cap bolts lightly, pry the crank fore-and-aft to align the thrust flanges, then torque
Spin the crankshaft at 500 RPM with an air drill while tightening the thrust cap bolts
rationale: Because the upper thrust bearing half sits in the block saddle and the lower thrust half sits in the removable main cap, torquing the cap down without aligning them can leave one flange slightly proud of the other. Snugging the cap lightly and prying the crankshaft forcefully fore-and-aft (leaving pry pressure forward while tightening) forces the thrust faces of both bearing halves into exact parallel alignment so the entire 360-degree thrust surface shares the axial load.

question: An engine uses Torque-To-Yield (TTY) cylinder head bolts with a specification of 'Torque to 30 lb-ft, then rotate an additional 90 degrees.' Technician A says that TTY bolts are designed to be reused indefinitely as long as the threads are wire-brushed and coated with anti-seize. Technician B says that the 90-degree angle turn means tightening the bolt to 90 lb-ft on a click-type torque wrench. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Neither technician is correct. Torque-To-Yield (TTY) bolts are permanently stretched into their plastic yield zone when tightened and must be replaced with new bolts whenever removed (reusing them risks bolt breakage or head gasket clamping failure). Furthermore, 'rotate an additional 90 degrees' is a rotational angle measurement (1/4 turn using a torque angle gauge), not 90 lb-ft of torque.

question: When installing main bearing inserts into an engine block and main bearing caps, the technician notices that half of the shells in the box have an oil hole and an internal oil groove, while the other half are completely smooth (un-grooved). Unless specifically instructed otherwise by the manufacturer, where are the grooved bearing shells with oil holes installed?
options: Both grooved shells on the #1 front main journal and both smooth shells on the #5 rear journal
In the removable lower main bearing caps where downward combustion load is highest
In the upper block saddles so the bearing oil holes match the main gallery ports
In either upper or lower positions randomly because main bearings are fed through the cap bolts
rationale: Pressurized oil is fed to the crankshaft from the main oil gallery drilled inside the engine block webbing.
