Recharge the battery to ≥75% (≥12.4V) first so a low battery does not falsely fail
Replace the starter motor and alternator before attempting to charge the battery
rationale: An open-circuit voltage of 11.95 Volts indicates the battery is nearly completely discharged (0–10% State of Charge; a 75% charged 12V lead-acid battery reads at least 12.4 V, and 100% is 12.6+ V). A carbon-pile load test requires the battery to be at least 75% charged (>= 12.4 V) first, otherwise a good battery that was simply drained during engine repairs will falsely fail the load test.

question: While removing a warped cast-iron exhaust manifold from an aluminum cylinder head, the rear M8 steel stud snaps off 1/8 inch (3 mm) recessed inside the aluminum cylinder head boss. Which of the following is a safe, industry-accepted method for extracting the broken steel stud without ruining the soft aluminum head threads?
options: Cut a deep slot across both the broken stud and the surrounding aluminum exhaust port sealing surface with an angle grinder
Drill freehand at a 30-degree angle into the aluminum head casting with a 1/2-inch bit and pack the hole with RTV silicone
Hammer a brittle square extractor into an off-center hole until the extractor snaps off flush inside the stud
Bolt a drill-guide plate to adjacent holes and drill centered with a left-hand bit
rationale: Freehand drilling on a jagged broken steel stud inside a soft aluminum head almost always causes the drill bit to walk off the hard steel and gouge into the soft aluminum threads. Bolting a hardened centering drill-guide template to the adjacent exhaust manifold holes keeps the left-hand drill bit dead-center in the stud (or alternatively, MIG-welding a washer and hex nut onto the steel stud safely concentrates intense thermal shock into the steel stud—since weld metal will not stick to aluminum—allowing the stud to be backed out with a wrench).

question: After installing a remanufactured V6 engine and bolting the transmission bellhousing flush to the block, the technician turns the ignition key to ON and notices the MIL (Check Engine Light) does not illuminate, the scan tool cannot communicate with the PCM, and the 15A PCM/Sensor 5-Volt reference fuse blows immediately upon replacement. Which post-installation error is the MOST likely cause?
options: The replacement spin-on oil filter was pre-filled with clean motor oil prior to installation
The new iridium spark plugs were gapped 0.005 in. wider than factory specification
The cooling system thermostat was installed without its rubber perimeter O-ring seal
The main harness was pinched between the bellhousing and block, shorting to ground
rationale: A classic complication during engine or transmission R&R is routing part of the engine loom across the top of the bellhousing dowel area or cylinder head flange where it gets pinched and crushed when the bellhousing or manifold bolts are torqued down. This shorts internal 12V feed or 5V reference wires directly to the grounded engine block, blowing the PCM fuse and killing scan tool communication.

question: A customer complains of a sharp single-cylinder misfire on Cylinder #3 that occurs ONLY under heavy load (such as accelerating up a hill in high gear), with no misfire at idle. Upon removing the Coil-On-Plug (COP) ignition unit and spark plug from Cylinder #3, the technician observes a thin, jagged black line running vertically down the white ceramic insulator of the spark plug and a matching burned grey track inside the rubber coil boot. What must be done to permanently repair this misfire?
options: Spray the spark plug insulator with brake cleaner and reuse both the original plug and rubber coil boot
Use a scan tool to reduce fuel injector pulse width by 25% on Cylinder #3
Replace BOTH the carbon-tracked spark plug and the rubber coil boot
Replace the three-way catalytic converter and downstream oxygen sensor
rationale: High-voltage secondary ignition energy always seeks the path of least electrical resistance to ground. When cylinder pressure spikes under heavy load, firing kV demand rises; if high voltage arcs down the outside of the porcelain insulator ("flashover"), it burns a conductive carbon path into BOTH the spark plug ceramic and the silicone rubber coil boot. If you replace only the spark plug and reuse the carbon-tracked boot, the old boot will immediately burn a new carbon track onto the brand-new spark plug!

question: Technician A says that as a spark plug's electrode gap wears wider over 100,000 miles of service, the secondary ignition voltage (firing kV) required to ionize the gap increases, placing higher dielectric stress on the ignition coil and boot insulation. Technician B says that a lean air-fuel mixture or high cylinder compression pressure lowers the required firing voltage (kV) to nearly zero. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Technician A is correct: a wider spark plug gap increases electrical resistance across the electrodes, driving firing voltage (kV) higher and stressing the coil and boot insulation. Technician B is incorrect: both a lean air-fuel mixture (fewer conductive ions) and high cylinder compression pressure (higher gas density between the electrodes) *increase* gap resistance and drive required firing kV significantly higher, not lower.

question: While removing the ignition coils on a DOHC 4-cylinder engine to diagnose a random misfire code (P0300), the technician discovers that the spark plug wells in the center of the valve cover are filled with 2 inches of engine oil, submerging the rubber coil boots. What causes engine oil to enter the spark plug wells on this design?
options: A leaking exhaust manifold flange gasket on the side of the cylinder head
Worn piston oil control rings pumping crankcase oil up through the spark plug threads
Overfilling the automatic transmission fluid level by one pint on the dipstick
Hardened, leaking spark plug tube seals pressed into the underside of the valve cover
rationale: On DOHC engines where the spark plugs are located down deep vertical tubes passing through the center of the valve cover, circular elastomer spark plug tube seals seal the valve cover against the cylinder head tubes. When these rubber seals harden with age and heat, splash oil from the camshafts leaks into the spark plug wells, swelling and degrading the rubber COP boots and causing high-voltage misfires.

question: After replacing a rear main crankshaft oil seal that includes an integrated magnetic multi-pole Crankshaft Position (CKP) reluctor ring (or after accidentally dropping a slotted steel crankshaft tone wheel during a rebuild), the engine cranks normally with good compression, fuel pressure, and cam timing, but sets DTC P0336 (CKP Sensor Range/Performance) and misfires erratically. Using a lab scope on the CKP sensor, the technician sees an irregular amplitude anomaly at the exact same point once every crankshaft revolution. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A bent tooth on the CKP reluctor wheel or a magnetic encoder seal pressed crooked
A restricted pleated-paper air filter element inside the air cleaner housing
A low R-134a refrigerant charge inside the air conditioning condenser
A carbon-fouled downstream heated oxygen sensor behind the catalytic converter
rationale: Modern engines rely on precise tooth spacing on the CKP reluctor wheel (such as a 60-minus-2 or 36-minus-1 tooth pattern) to calculate crankshaft speed, ignition timing, and misfire detection down to fractions of a degree. If a reluctor tooth is bent by a prybar during flywheel removal, or if a magnetic polymer encoder ring is scratched, touched with a magnet, or pressed to the wrong depth, the CKP waveform distorts once per revolution (360°), causing false misfire detection or a no-start.

question: A technician is diagnosing a Gasoline Direct Injection (GDI) engine that cranks and starts, runs in a reduced-power "limp-home" mode with a maximum speed of 3,000 RPM, and sets DTC P0087 (Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low). On the scan tool, the Low-Pressure fuel sensor reads 65 psi (specification is 60–70 psi), and the High-Pressure Fuel Rail sensor also reads 65 psi at idle and under load (specification is 500–2,200 psi). What does this data indicate?
options: The in-tank electric low-pressure lift pump has failed completely and delivers 0 psi
The vehicle fuel tank is completely empty and the fuel gauge sender is stuck at half tank
The lift pump supplies 65 psi base pressure, but the cam-driven HPFP builds no high pressure
The GDI piezo fuel injectors are stuck operating at 5,000 psi rail pressure at idle
rationale: A GDI fuel system has two stages: an electric in-tank low-pressure lift pump (~50–75 psi) that feeds a camshaft-driven mechanical High-Pressure Fuel Pump (~500–2,900+ psi). When the high-pressure fuel rail reads the exact same 65 psi as the low-pressure supply line, the engine is running solely on in-tank lift pump pressure ("limp mode") because the HPFP spill control solenoid is stuck open/unpowered or the mechanical HPFP plunger/cam follower has failed.

question: While removing the cylinder head on a Gasoline Direct Injection (GDI) engine, the technician pulls the high-pressure fuel injectors out of their bores in the cylinder head. When reinstalling the original GDI fuel injectors, what critical sealing procedure MUST be followed to prevent combustion gas blow-by and high-pressure fuel leaks?
options: Wrap the nozzle tip of each GDI fuel injector in three layers of household plumber's thread tape
Replace the white PTFE tip seal using the expander/mandrel tools plus the upper O-rings
Coat the white PTFE combustion seal heavily with chassis grease and hammer the injector into the cylinder head bore
Reuse all original O-rings and Teflon tip seals without brushing carbon out of the injector bore
rationale: Because the tip of a GDI injector protrudes directly into the combustion chamber (1,000+ psi combustion pressures and intense heat), it uses a specialized PTFE (Teflon) combustion seal ring at the nozzle tip in addition to the upper high-pressure fuel rail O-ring. Whenever a GDI injector is removed, a new Teflon seal must be slid over a tapered cone tool and compressed back to exact bore diameter with a sizing sleeve (and installed dry, never oiled, so oil doesn't carbonize in the bore).

question: Before disconnecting a high-pressure fuel line or fuel rail on a warm Gasoline Direct Injection (GDI) engine, why must the technician follow the manufacturer's pressure bleed-down procedure (such as disabling the in-tank pump/HPFP and running the engine until it stalls, or waiting for rail pressure to decay while monitoring the High-Pressure Fuel Rail PID on a scan tool) while wearing safety glasses?
options: Gasoline Direct Injection fuel rails operate under 25 in. Hg of vacuum after hot shutdown
Loosening a high-pressure fuel line allows outside air to enter the engine oil pump pickup tube
Residual GDI pressure can exceed 1,500–3,000+ psi, risking skin injection or fire
Cracking open a GDI fuel line erases the learned camshaft phaser adaptations in the PCM
rationale: Unlike traditional port fuel injection (45–60 psi), GDI high-pressure fuel rails operate between 500 psi and 3,000+ psi. Furthermore, after hot shutdown, engine heat soaking into the sealed aluminum fuel rail causes trapped fuel to expand thermally, spiking rail pressure even higher; cracking open a fitting under 2,000+ psi poses a severe skin-injection and fire hazard.

question: A turbocharged 4-cylinder engine suffered a seized turbocharger center shaft bearing at 85,000 miles. A technician installed a brand-new replacement turbocharger cartridge, changed the engine oil and filter, and primed the turbo with oil—yet the brand-new turbocharger seized its shaft bearing again after only 45 miles of highway driving. What critical component in the turbocharger lubrication supply circuit did the technician most likely fail to replace or inspect?
options: The fine-mesh oil strainer screen in the turbo feed banjo bolt/line was plugged
The downstream heated oxygen sensor mounted behind the catalytic converter was not recalibrated
The intake manifold runner control (IMRC) vacuum actuator diaphragm was left unplugged
The rubber charge-air cooler (intercooler) outlet coupling hose clamp was over-tightened
rationale: Many turbocharged engines house a tiny, fine-mesh metallic strainer screen inside the oil feed line fitting or hollow banjo bolt at the engine block/cylinder head gallery. When carbonized oil sludge plugs this screen, it starves and destroys the original turbocharger; if the technician bolts on a new turbo without replacing or cleaning the oil supply pipe, banjo bolt screen, and oil return drain tube, the new turbocharger is immediately starved of oil and fails within miles.

question: Many multi-valve engines use an Intake Manifold Runner Control (IMRC) system—or Variable Intake Manifold (VIM) / Tumble Generator Valve (TGV) flaps—controlled by a vacuum or electric actuator. How would a vehicle behave if the IMRC runner flaps become broken or stuck in the CLOSED (long/restricted runner) position on both banks?
options: Loss of low-RPM swirl/tumble causing a rough cold idle and misfire, with normal high-RPM top-end power
The engine will idle at 4,500 RPM with the throttle closed
Normal idle/low-end torque, but severe power loss above 3,500–4,000 RPM at WOT
Excessive exhaust backpressure ahead of the catalytic converter
rationale: Intake Manifold Runner Control (IMRC) systems keep the secondary runner flaps closed at idle and low RPM to force air through longer/narrower primary passages, increasing air velocity, tumble, and low-end torque. Above ~3,500 RPM, the PCM opens the flaps to uncover short, high-flow runners for maximum volumetric efficiency; therefore, flaps stuck closed choke off high-RPM breathing (normal idle, no top-end power), whereas flaps stuck open reduce low-speed swirl/tumble and cause cold-idle roughness/lean misfires.

question: Technician A says that if a turbocharger's exhaust wastegate valve becomes mechanically stuck in the OPEN position, exhaust gases will bypass the turbine wheel continuously, resulting in sluggish acceleration, severe turbo lag, and an underboost DTC (such as P0299). Technician B says that if the wastegate actuator diaphragm ruptures or the wastegate valve sticks CLOSED on a conventional pressure-actuated wastegate, the turbocharger will produce excessive boost pressure (overboost DTC P0234) and trigger PCM fuel/throttle cut. Who is correct?
options: Technician A only
Technician B only
Both Technician A and Technician B
Neither Technician A nor Technician B
rationale: Both technicians are correct. The turbocharger wastegate regulates boost pressure by bypassing exhaust gas around the turbine wheel once target boost is reached. If the wastegate sticks open (or if a vacuum-operated electronic wastegate loses vacuum supply), exhaust energy bypasses the turbine from idle onward, causing low boost (P0299). Conversely, if a pressure-actuated wastegate sticks closed or its boost reference hose splits, all exhaust gas drives the turbine unchecked, causing dangerous overboost (P0234).

question: A turbocharged engine exhibits a loud "whooshing" air hiss under acceleration, lacks power, blows black smoke under load, and sets DTC P0299 (Turbocharger Underboost) along with negative Long-Term Fuel Trim (-18%) under boost. To locate the fault, the technician installs stepped plugs in the turbo inlet pipe and throttle body inlet, pressurizes the intake charge pipes and Charge Air Cooler (intercooler) to 15 psi with regulated shop air and smoke, and finds air roaring out of a split plastic end-tank seam on the intercooler. Why did this boost leak cause negative (-18%) fuel trims under load?
options: Metered boost air escaped before reaching the cylinders, leaving excess fuel (rich)
Unmeasured outside air was sucked into the intercooler split while under 15 psi of positive boost pressure
The charge-air intercooler leaks engine antifreeze directly into the upstream oxygen sensor bung
The wide-band upstream air-fuel ratio sensor measures manifold boost pressure instead of exhaust oxygen
rationale: On a MAF-equipped turbocharged engine, when the system is in vacuum (at idle), a leak downstream of the MAF sucks in unmeasured air and causes a lean condition (+ fuel trim). However, under positive boost (10–20 psi), air already metered by the MAF sensor blows out through the split intercooler or charge boot into the atmosphere; the PCM injects fuel for air that never reached the cylinders, causing a rich condition, negative fuel trims (-18%), and loss of boost pressure.

question: On a vehicle equipped with a positive-displacement Roots or twin-screw mechanical supercharger driven directly by the crankshaft pulley, what is the purpose of the vacuum/electronically controlled Supercharger Bypass Valve during idle and light-load highway cruising?
options: It mechanically uncouples the crankshaft harmonic balancer from the primary timing chain at idle
It routes hot exhaust gas from the catalytic converter directly into the supercharger rotor housing
It recirculates air across the rotors without boost, cutting drag and heat at cruise
It sprays pressurized engine coolant onto the supercharger ribbed serpentine drive belt
rationale: Because a belt-driven positive-displacement supercharger displaces a fixed volume of air with every crankshaft revolution, compressing air when the driver is merely idling or cruising at light throttle wastes significant horsepower and heats the intake charge. The supercharger bypass valve stays open under high manifold vacuum (idle/cruise) to equalize pressure across the rotors, and closes immediately when manifold vacuum drops (heavy throttle) so full boost is delivered to the cylinders.

question: A V6 engine with a molded composite upper and lower intake manifold exhibits a rough idle, hesitation, and lean misfire codes (P0171/P0300) for the first 3 minutes after a cold morning start at 35°F (2°C). Once the engine warms up to 160°F (71°C), the misfire disappears completely and short-term fuel trims return to ±2%. Using a smoke machine on the intake manifold when the engine is hot reveals zero leaks. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Burned exhaust valve faces on all six cylinders that seal tightly once the catalytic converter lights off
A jumped Bank 1 camshaft timing chain that automatically re-indexes itself once engine oil warms up
Hardened intake gaskets that leak cold and swell shut as the castings warm up
A permanently kinked fuel return line raising port fuel rail pressure to 110 psi at cold idle
rationale: Silicone and fluoroelastomer intake manifold runner O-rings compress and lose elasticity ('compression set') over years of heat cycling. When the aluminum cylinder head and plastic intake manifold are cold and contracted, a microscopic gap opens between the flange and hardened gasket—admitting unmetered air at cold idle. As the engine warms up, thermal expansion of the castings and rubber closes the gap, which is why intake smoke or propane testing for this complaint must be performed on a completely cold engine.

question: While diagnosing an engine that idles very roughly, shakes, and stalls whenever shifted into Drive—yet smooths out completely and runs well above 2,000 RPM—a technician measures only 9 in. Hg of intake manifold vacuum at idle. When the technician removes the Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve and inspects its pintle, a hard chunk of carbon is found wedged under the pintle seat, holding the EGR valve slightly OPEN at idle. Why does an EGR valve stuck open cause a rough idle and stalling?
options: The EGR valve pintle position sensor shuts off electric fuel pump voltage at idle
Exhaust gas recirculation raises peak combustion chamber flame temperatures by 1,000°F at idle
An open EGR pintle physically blocks exhaust gas from exiting through the rear muffler
Inert exhaust gas enters at idle, diluting the small idle charge like a vacuum leak
rationale: EGR systems are designed to remain completely closed at idle, during cold warm-up, and at wide-open throttle, opening only during warm part-throttle cruise. If carbon holds the EGR pintle open at idle, inert exhaust gas (CO2 and N2) floods the intake plenum, lowering manifold vacuum and diluting the air-fuel mixture so severely that it cannot burn reliably, causing a rough misfire and stall that disappears once throttle airflow increases at higher RPM.

question: How will a gasoline engine respond during warm, part-throttle highway acceleration if its Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) passages inside the intake manifold become completely plugged with carbon (preventing any inert exhaust gas from entering the cylinders)?
options: Crankcase oil pressure drops to 0 psi whenever the throttle plate opens past 30%
The engine stalls repeatedly at every stoplight due to excessive inert exhaust gas dilution
Combustion chamber temperatures drop so low at highway cruise that spark plugs foul with ice
Peak combustion temperatures rise under load, causing spark knock and high NOx
rationale: The primary function of the EGR system is to introduce a small, metered amount of inert exhaust gas into the intake charge during warm part-throttle load to absorb combustion heat and keep peak flame temperatures below the 2,500°F (1,370°C) threshold where atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen combine to form $\text{NO}_x$. If the EGR passages plug with carbon (or the valve sticks closed), combustion temperatures spike under load, causing audible detonation (pinging), high $\text{NO}_x$ emissions, and often an EGR low-flow DTC (P0401).

question: On many inline-6, V6, and V8 engines with long cast-iron or tubular exhaust manifolds bolted to aluminum cylinder heads, the frontmost and rearmost exhaust manifold bolts/studs frequently shear off over time, causing a cold-start exhaust tick. Why do the end studs fail repeatedly, and what must be checked before installing a new exhaust manifold gasket and studs?
options: High engine oil pressure inside the exhaust manifold passages stretches the end mounting bolts
Thermal cycling warps the manifold ends; check flatness with a straightedge and resurface
The upstream oxygen sensor wire pulls downward on the front manifold stud with 500 lbs of force
Cast-aluminum cylinder heads shrink by 0.250 in. in length the first time the engine reaches 200°F
rationale: Cast-iron exhaust manifolds reach 1,000–1,400°F under load and expand at a different rate than the water-cooled aluminum cylinder head. Over thousands of heat cycles, the manifold permanently warps and bows at its outer ends, shearing off the end studs. Simply extracting the broken stud and installing a new gasket without checking the manifold flange with a straightedge (and resurfacing or replacing a warped manifold) will cause the new stud or gasket to fail again shortly.

question: A vehicle sets DTC P0420 (Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold - Bank 1). Before condemning the expensive three-way catalytic converter, a technician monitors both the upstream Air-Fuel/O2 sensor (B1S1) and the downstream O2 sensor (B1S2) on a graphing scan tool at 2,000 RPM, and performs a physical inspection. All of the following conditions MUST be ruled out before replacing a catalytic converter EXCEPT:
options: Pinhole exhaust leaks at the exhaust manifold flange, flex pipe, or around the oxygen sensor bungs that draw in false ambient oxygen
Engine oil consumption, coolant consumption (silicone poisoning), or chronic ignition misfires that have overheated or contaminated the catalyst substrate
A worn cabin air filter element behind the glovebox
Lazy or skewed upstream/downstream oxygen sensors or uncorrected fuel trim imbalances
rationale: Catalytic converters rarely die of "old age"—they are almost always damaged by an upstream engine problem (misfires dumping raw fuel that melts the ceramic monolith, burning oil/phosphorus coating the washcoat, or silicon from coolant/non-sensor-safe RTV poisoning the catalyst) or falsely condemned due to an exhaust leak near the O2 sensors. The HVAC cabin air filter affects only passenger compartment ventilation and has zero connection to the engine or exhaust system.

question: When installing a new embossed multi-layer steel (MLS) or laminated graphite-over-perforated-steel exhaust manifold gasket that has one smooth shiny metal side and one textured/embossed side, how are directional exhaust manifold gaskets and their retaining hardware properly installed?
options: Follow 'MANIFOLD SIDE' markings, use new hardware, and torque from the center outward
Coat both sides of the MLS exhaust gasket with 1/4 inch of blue RTV silicone and impact-tighten from the ends inward
Soak the metallic exhaust gasket in water and reuse stretched, corroded manifold studs without cleaning the threads
Stack two exhaust manifold gaskets on top of each other to compensate for a 0.045 in. warped manifold flange
rationale: Directional laminated exhaust manifold gaskets are engineered so the smooth metallic heat-shield face allows the cast-iron exhaust manifold to expand and slide slightly across the gasket during 1,300°F thermal cycles without tearing the graphite core against the cylinder head. Furthermore, RTV silicone burns away at exhaust temperatures and contaminates oxygen sensors, and stacking gaskets fails rapidly—warped manifolds exceeding ~0.004–0.006 in. must be resurfaced flat and torqued from the center outward.
